Be careful with this:

1) It's published on biorxiv, which is open source and not peer reviewed. Literally anyone can post here. Publication here doesn't make it correct or authoritative.

2) There are 4 short sequences. Mathematically, it's essentially a given they would find a match in a BLAST search. Individually, they don't mean much of anything. These sequences are found in literally hundreds of viruses, let alone other species. The problem with bioinformatics is that it can be a bit of a fishing expedition without some very serious controls - and these guys didn't use any of those techniques.

3) The unique structure of the 3D-modeled protein is interesting, but remember that HIV-1 targets CD4-T-cells (your immune cells) using gp120. This virus does not appear to do that. It targets the lung, so having the gp120 segment may be meaningless since it doesn't affect function.

Please let knowledgeable people look more closely at this. I have some experience with bioinformatics, but am not qualified to comment more than what I've put forward above. Simply put, we need more information. Even if this proves to be true, it needs to be validated by a 2nd team, and the modeling they've done on a computer needs to be confirmed with living cells in a lab.

4) Reports of HIV drugs being given are circulating. There will be ineffective. Only 2 drugs attack the outside of the HIV virus. One attacks a protein called gp41 (not gp120). The other attacks the target on the T-cell called CCR5. Neither would work on this segment of the HIV virus. All other HIV drugs work on specific proteins within the HIV lifecycle and would have no effect on the coronavirus since it does not contain those proteins.
